tier_reason: Chapter11/11_scopeguard_te_benchmark.C is public Google Benchmark code that times ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast against the std::function guard (ScopeGuardTypeErased), the template guard and explicit delete, but the file has no comments or results and the repo carries no build line, flags or CPU; the ns figures exist only in the book (first-party), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Book (relayed via the seed lead from the book; no numbers anywhere in the repo): buffer-based guard 5.48 ns against 6.29 ns for the std::function guard in the null-pointer case (rand() call, pointer stays null; BM_nodelete_* rows by the book's description), and 12.7 ns against 13.4 ns when always allocating (BM_delete_* rows); explicit delete 4.48 and 4.54 ns. About 1.15x and 1.06x, i.e. 0.8 and 0.7 ns saved per guard (derived from the relayed numbers).
corrections.workload: Google Benchmark of a scope guard that deletes a pointer: ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast (16-byte alignas(8) inline buffer plus a function-pointer invoker) against a guard holding a std::function<void()>, the template ScopeGuard and a hand-written explicit delete, in four cases: noop (guard on a null pointer created outside the loop), nodelete (rand() call, pointer stays null), nodelete2 (two pointers, 16-byte capture) and delete (rand() call plus new int and delete every iteration). All guards capture by reference ([&]).
corrections.caveats: Marginal gain (6 to 15%, under 1 ns per guard). By reading the source (not compiled or run here), ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast declares its own 'mutable bool commit_' that shadows CommitFlag::commit_, so commit() (which sets the base flag) does not suppress the cleanup, and the defaulted move constructor copies the derived flag as false, so a moved-from guard still fires (the cleanup would run twice): the fast guard is not behaviourally equivalent to the std::function guard, and the benchmark never calls commit() or moves a guard, so the timing does not show it. Narrower than the baseline: static_asserts that the callable is trivially copyable, trivially destructible and at most 16 bytes, has no heap fallback, and an lvalue callable fails to compile because Callable deduces to a reference type. The benchmarked [&] lambdas (8 or 16 bytes, trivially copyable) also fit std::function's small-object storage in libstdc++ and libc++, so neither guard allocates and the gap is std::function's extra manager and invoker indirection only. The template ScopeGuard (separate entry) beats this guard in both cases (4.50 and 4.56 ns relayed), so the buffer guard only matters where type erasure is needed. Baseline is the book's own std::function guard, not a library guard. Compiler, flags, standard library and CPU not stated, first-party, teaching code rather than a packaged library. Tier C. File opened: Chapter11/11_scopeguard_te_benchmark.C.
